blocks.text: Now, to reply to the objections: Fuller denies that there is anything in the nature of the hedgehog that suits the kippod. This I cannot sufficiently wonder at, since Isaiah and Zephaniah always describe the kippod as a solitary animal and φιλέρημον [phileremon], dwelling in the desolate cities of Babylon, Bozrah and Nineveh. That the hedgehog is such, there is no one who does not know: ζῶον χῆρον, ἤτοι ἔρημον [zōon chēron, ētoi erēmon], an animal which its spines, which no one touches with impunity, keep from all society with other animals. Hence it came about that in Greek it was called χὴρ [chēr]. Hesychius: χήρ· ἐχῖνος [chēr: echinos], namely from χηρώσις [chērōsis], that is, ἐρημώσις [erēmōsis]. Hence also the Latin name; not ab haerendo [from clinging] or horrendo [from bristling], as some would have it. For just as hir for vola manus [the palm of the hand] in Probus and Charisius was made from the Greek χεὶρ [cheir], so her for hericius [hedgehog] comes entirely from the Greek χήρ [chēr]. The animal which a later age, as the word grew longer, called herix, hericius, herinacius, the ancients called her. Nemesianus in the Cynegetica:
And the hedgehog wrapped up in the fold of its spiny body.
And long before, Plautus in the Captivi, Act 1, as emended by the distinguished Salmasius:
Go now, hunt a hare: now you hold a hedgehog.

Or, if by the name kippod in the Prophets we understand the porcupine (which [?] [col. 1040] we have proved from the ancients to be included in the same genus as the hedgehog), the matter will seem[?]

[II, 459] all the more fitted to inspire horror, if the Prophets threaten that populous cities, such as Babylon among the Chaldeans, Nineveh among the Assyrians, and Bozrah among the Idumaeans, will pass as an inheritance to porcupines. For the porcupine is both larger and fiercer than the hedgehog, and, because of the missile spines which it hurls at dogs and hunters with a sure and well-aimed stroke, far more terrible ^{(1)}. Accordingly the excellent Poet, after vividly describing the porcupine bristling with hairs sharp like arrows, teaches in these words how far the porcupine surpasses the echinus, that is, the hedgehog:

But this array does not stay fixed, in the manner of the woodland hedgehog. It fights on the offensive with frequent volleys, and guards its limbs from afar, and, whirled through the air, its native missile flies out from its shaken back.
And whereas Ion in the Phoenix ^{a)} mocks the οἰζυρὰς τέχνας [oizyras technas], the wretched arts, of the hedgehog, which, when attacked by other beasts,

Στρόβιλον ἀμφ' ἄκανθαν εἰλίξας δέμας, Κεῖται δακεῖν τε καὶ θιγεῖν ἀμήχανος· [Strobilon amph' akanthan eilixas demas, keitai dakein te kai thigein amēchanos] Keeping its body under a dense ball of thorns, it lies there, unable to bite or to touch in return:
the porcupine's courage and skill in fighting so carried the most illustrious Poet away in admiration that it drew these verses from him:

Sometimes, fleeing in the manner of the Parthians, it wounds its pursuer: sometimes, as if pitching camp in order, it lashes out its terrifying point in a dense wave, and roughens its shoulders with kindred shafts. The whole body of the beast does battle, and its back, shaken, resounds with a harsh crash; you would think columns roused by the goad of trumpets were clashing with standards joined. So great a din rages in so small a space. To its arms is added cunning, and a fear sparing of itself, and an anger never prodigal of its darts, cautiously content to threaten, and spending its shots only to save its life. Error is absent; skill directs a sure stroke, the distance never deceiving its measure; and the mute skin keeps its course and guides the efforts of a practised eye.
And a little later,

Behold, a small beast is armed with its own weapons, and seeks no outside help; it carries everything with it; [II, 460] it is its own quiver, its own javelin, its own bow. One animal possesses all the arts of war.
Finally he concludes that we learned the art of shooting from this beast. And of the same the emperor Hadrian:
With missile spines it kept dogs and men far off, and put them all to flight.
And Phile, ch. 59, On Animals:

Ὕστριξ δὲ τὰς ἄνωθεν ἐκπέμπει τρίχας, Ἃς ἡ φύσις γ᾽ ἔθηξε καὶ πρὸ τῆς μάχης. Φρίξασα γὰρ τὰ νῶτα βάλλει τοὺς πέλους Οἷον ἀπὸ νευρᾶς εὐτυχῶν ^{b)} τις τοξότης. [Hystrix de tas anōthen ekpempei trichas, has hē physis g' ethēxe kai pro tēs machēs. Phrixasa gar ta nōta ballei tous pelous hoion apo neuras eutychōn tis toxotēs.] As the rough porcupine hurls its hairs like darts, which shrewd nature has sharpened for battle, for when it draws in its back, as with a bowstring drawn taut, it hurls darts at its enemies from afar.
And Oppian, book 3 of the Cynegetica, v. 398:

— — — Θοὰς δ᾽ ἔφριξεν ἐθείρας
Καί τ᾽ ὀπίσω νώτοισιν ἀκαχμένον ὠκυπέτῃσιν
Ἰθὺς ἀκοντίζει μαλερὸν βέλος. — — [Thoas d' ephrixen etheiras kai t' opisō nōtoisin akachmenon ōkypetēisin ithys akontizei maleron belos.]
It raises its sharp spines, and shoots straight backwards the deadly dart fixed on its swift-flying back. And a little later,
Δηθάκις ἔκτεινεν κύνα κάρχαρον, [Dēthakis ekteinen kyna karcharon,]
